text: Hinton's fix is a temperature T in the softmax, applied to the teacher and the student alike during training: q i = exp(z i / T) / Σ j exp(z j / T) L = (1 − α) · CE(y, q (T=1) ) + α · T 2 · KL(p teacher (T) ‖ q student (T) ) z i the logit of token i ; T = 1 is the ordinary softmax, higher T flattens it y the true next token (the hard label), when there is one T 2 "the magnitudes of the gradients produced by the soft targets scale as 1/T 2 ", so the soft term is multiplied by T 2 to keep the mix stable as T changes; Hinton found "a considerably lower weight" on the hard term worked best (§2) Try: real next-token logits from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, saved from a run on this page's data script.

text: Forward or reverse KL A student that is smaller than its teacher cannot match it everywhere, so the choice of what to minimise decides where it is wrong.
label: core
key: Forward or reverse KL A student

text: With teacher distribution p and student q : forward KL(p ‖ q) = Σ x p(x) log [p(x) / q(x)] reverse KL(q ‖ p) = Σ x q(x) log [q(x) / p(x)] forward expectation under the teacher: punishes the student for missing anything the teacher considers likely, so it covers every mode, even if that means putting mass between them reverse expectation under the student: punishes the student for putting mass where the teacher puts little, so it seeks one mode and ignores the rest Classic logit distillation and SFT on teacher samples both minimise forward KL.
label: core

text: MiniLLM argued that for generation this is the wrong way round: forward KL makes the student "overestimate the low-probability regions of the teacher distribution", which when sampled produce text the teacher would never write, so it switched to reverse KL.
label: core

text: GKD treats the divergence as a choice ("useful when the student lacks the expressivity to mimic the teacher's distribution") and in its own experiments picked differently per task: a generalised Jensen-Shannon divergence for translation, forward KL for summarisation and arithmetic (Figure 1).
label: core

text: For pretraining-style logit distillation of a pruned model, Minitron measured the opposite of MiniLLM: forward KL reached an LM loss of 2.155 against 2.665 for reverse KL (Table 16).
label: core

text: Thinking Machines chose reverse KL for on-policy distillation because it is "mode seeking": "it learns one specific behavior (the teacher's) instead of spreading its distribution across several suboptimal options" ( blog ).
label: core

text: Whose text: off-policy against on-policy Sequence-level and logit distillation both train on text the teacher wrote (or a fixed corpus).

key: Whose text: off-policy against on-policy Sequence-level

text: That is off-policy : at serving time the student continues from its own previous tokens, and the first time it drifts off the teacher's path it is somewhere training never showed it.
label: core

text: Errors compound, a problem known as exposure bias .
label: core

text: GKD's diagnosis: "current KD methods for auto-regressive sequence models suffer from distribution mismatch between output sequences seen during training and those generated by the student during inference" ( Agarwal et al. ).
label: core

text: On-policy distillation fixes the mismatch the way reinforcement learning does: the student writes the text, then the teacher grades every token of it.
label: core

text: It keeps RL's relevance (training happens exactly where the student goes) and adds what RL lacks, a dense signal: one teacher opinion per token instead of one reward per answer.
label: core

text: Thinking Machines' recipe sets each token's advantage to the negative reverse KL, estimated from the teacher's log-probability of the token the student sampled, with "a discount factor of zero", and runs it through an ordinary RL loss ( blog ).
label: core

text: GKD and Qwen3 match the teacher's full distribution at every student position instead.
label: core
key: match the teacher's full distribution at every student position

text: Whose text turns out to matter less than which divergence.
label: core

text: A controlled strong-to-weak study varied rollout policy, token-level KL direction and learning rate one at a time (Llama3 and Qwen2.5 students; scientific, medical and arithmetic reasoning) and found that "rollout policy does not necessarily play a central role": KL direction shaped accuracy and output coverage, and learning rate governed forgetting and update sparsity.
label: core
key: rollout policy does not necessarily play a central role

text: Forward KL was "remarkably robust to rollout policy"; reverse KL "is substantially more sensitive and favours student-generated rollouts".
label: core

text: Cui et al. find that on-policy distillation "improves performance without expanding the student's capabilities": when the implicit reward is reliable it makes correct answers easier to sample; when it misaligns with quality, the student collapses into excessively long, repetitive output that the teacher scores well, which is reward hacking of the teacher ( Reward Hacking ).
label: core

text: Masking such unhealthy responses during training, or starting from an SFT checkpoint, each mitigated the collapse ( Gains and Collapse in OPD (arXiv 2610.03185) ).
label: core

text: Real tokenizations from this page's data script: With different splits there is no position at which to compare, so across families you either distil at the sequence level (generated text works with any tokenizer) or use a cross-tokenizer loss such as ULD, which "uses optimal transport theory to enable distillation across different architectures and tokenizers" ( Boizard et al. ).
label: core
key: Real tokenizations from this page's data

text: For on-policy distillation across tokenizers, more alignment is not better: across three teacher-student pairs with different tokenizers (maths and code), strict 1:1 aligned positions already covered most student tokens, reverse KL on a student-selected top-16 of the shared vocabulary at those positions matched full shared-vocabulary distillation, and adding span-level supervision to reach complete coverage reduced accuracy, because those weakly aligned gradients disagree with the strict ones ( Rethinking Cross-Tokenizer OPD (arXiv 2610.08448) ).
label: depth
